¶
{{smaller block|Spending all the day, and a good part of the night, in dancing, carolling, and ''wassailing''.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.}}}}

'''wassail-bout''' (wos′ạ̄l-bout), ''n.'' Same as ''wassail'', 2.
{{smaller block|<poem>Many a ''wassail-bout''
Wore the long winter out.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Skeleton in Armor.}}}}

'''wassail-bowl''' (wos′ạ̄l-bōl), ''n.'' The bowl in which wassail was mixed and served.
{{smaller block|<poem>The woods, or some near town
That is a neighbour to the bordering down,
Hath drawn them thither, ’bout some lusty sport,
Or spiced ''wassail-bowl''.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, v. 1.}}}}

'''wassail-bread''' (wos′ạ̄l-bred), ''n.'' Bread eaten at a wassail.

'''wassail-candle''' (wos′ạ̄l-kan″dl), ''n.'' A candle used at a wassail.

'''wassail-cup''' (wos′ạ̄l-kup), ''n.'' A cup from which wassail was drunk.

'''wassailer''' (wos′ạ̄l-ėr), ''n.'' One who takes part in a wassail or drinking-bout.
{{smaller block|<poem>The rudeness and swilled insolence
Of such late ''wassailers''.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 179.}}}}

'''wassail-horn''' (wos′ạ̄l-hôrn), ''n.'' A drinking-horn of the middle ages. {{smaller|The name is taken from the appearance of the word ''wassail'' in the silver-gilt mounting of an ancient horn preserved at Queen’s College, Oxford.}}

'''wassel''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''wassail''.

'''wasser†''' (wos′ėr), ''n.'' [Appar. < G. ''wasser'' = E. ''water'', perhaps through some popular myth imported from Germany. Cf. ''wasserman''.] A water-demon (?).

{{smaller block|<poem>The horrible huge whales did there appeare;
The ''wasser'' that makes maryners to feare.</poem>
{{right|''The Newe Metamorphosis'' (1600).}}}}

'''wasserman†''' (wos′ėr-man), ''n.'' [< G. ''wasser'', water, + ''mann'', man. Cf. E. dial. ''wassel-man'', a scarecrow. Cf. ''waterman''.] A male sea-monster of human form; a sort of merman.
{{smaller block|<poem>The griesly ''Wasserman'', that makes his game
The flying ships with swiftnes to pursew.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 24.}}}}

'''wasshe†''', ''v.'' An old spelling of ''wash''.

'''wast<sup>1</sup>''' (wost). See ''was''.

'''wast<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''waist''.

'''wastable''' (wās′ta-bl), ''a.'' [< ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] '''1.''' Liable to waste.
{{smaller block|For ale that is newe is ''wastable'' with-owten dowt.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 129.}}}}
'''2†.''' Wasteful.
{{smaller block|<poem>For much of this chaffare that is ''wastable''
Might be forborne for dere and deceiuable.</poem>
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 193.}}}}

'''wastage''' (wās′tāj), ''n.'' [< ''waste''<sup>1</sup> + ''-age''.] Loss by use, wear, decay, leakage, etc.; waste.
{{smaller block|The manufacture of it [shell money] was large and constant, to replace the continual ''wastage'' which was caused by the sacrifice of so much upon the death of wealthy men, and by the propitiatory sacrifices performed by many tribes, especially those of the Coast Range.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXVIII. 301.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There is a subtlety which here in Rome
Men look for in blind ''wastage'' of their lives,
Not knowing where to seek it.</poem>
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVIII. 178.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wassail|6833|waste}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|<poem>We did but . . . pledge you all
In ''wassail''.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, Prol.}}}}
'''2.''' A festive occasion or meeting where drinking and pledging of healths are indulged in; festivities; a drinking-bout; a carouse.
{{smaller block|<poem>The king doth wake to-night and takes his rouse,
Keeps ''wassail''.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 4. 9.}}}}
'''3.''' The liquor used on such occasions; specifically, ale, mixed with a smaller amount of wine, sweetened and flavored with spices, fruit, etc.
{{smaller block|''Wassail'', or rather the ''wassail'' bowl, . . . was a bowl of spiced ale formerly carried about by young women on New-year’s eve. {{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 466.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But let no footstep beat the floor,
Nor bowl of ''wassail'' mantle warm.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cv.}}}}
'''4†.''' A merry drinking-song.
{{smaller block|Have you done your ''wassail?'' ’tis a handsome drowsy ditty, I’ll assure you.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, iii. 1.}}}}
='''Syn. 2.''' ''Revel, Debauch'', etc. See ''carousal''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wassail''' (wos′āl), ''v.''   [Also ''wassel''; < ''wassail'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To drink to the health or prosperity of: as, to ''wassail'' the apple (an old custom on Christmas eve).
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wassaile'' the Trees, that they may beare
You many a Plum, and many a Peare;
For more or lesse fruits they will bring,
As you doe give them Wassailing.</poem>{{right|''Herrick'', Hesperides, Ceremonies for Christmas, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ceremony of ''wassailing'' the apple orchard on Twelfth Night is said to be obsolete.{{right|''The Academy'', April 19, 1890, p. 265.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To drink healths; carouse.

{{smaller block|Spending all the day, and a good part of the night, in dancing, carolling, and ''wassailing''.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.}}}}

'''waste'''<sup>1</sup> (wāst), ''a.''   [Formerly also ''wast;'' < ME. ''wast'', ''waast'', < OF. ''wast'', ''guast'', ''gast'', ''gaste'', waste (''faire wast'', make waste), < L. ''vastus'', waste, desolate, vast: see ''vast''. The word was confused with the ult. related early ME. ''weste'', < AS. ''wēste'' = OS. ''wōsti'' = OFries. ''woste'' = OHG. ''wuosti'', MHG. ''wuesti'', G. ''wüst'', waste, desolate: see ''waste''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1.''' Desert; desolate; uninhabited.
{{smaller block|<poem>So wide a forest and so ''waste'' as this,
Nor famous Ardeyn, nor fowle Arlo, is.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Astrophel, l. 95.}}}}
{{smaller block|He found him in a desert land, and in the ''waste'' howling wilderness. {{right|Deut. xxxii. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Far in the ''waste'' Soudan.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Epitaph on General Gordon.}}}}
'''2.''' In a state of desolation and decay; ruined; ruinous; blank; cheerless; dismal; dreary.
{{smaller block|Certayne old ''wast'' and broken howeses.
{{right|''Berners'', tr. of Froissart’s Chron., I. cclxix.}}}}
{{smaller block|I will make thee [Jerusalem] ''waste'', and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee.
{{right|Ezek. v. 14.}}}}
'''3.''' Unused; untilled; unproductive.
{{smaller block|It had layne ''wast'' two hundred yeares.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 159.}}}}
{{smaller block|Almost one-fourth of the cultivable land of a country which was held to be over-populated was lying ''waste''.
{{right|''W. S. Gregg'', Irish Hist. for Eng. Readers, p. 145.}}}}
'''4.''' Rejected as unfit for use, or spoiled in the using; refuse; hence, of little or no value; useless: as, ''waste'' paper; ''waste'' materials.—'''5†.''' Idle; empty; vain; of no value or significance. {{smaller block|<poem>Where is oure semely sone?
I trowe oure wittis be ''waste'' as wynde.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 157.}}}}
{{smaller block|He hath maad mi covenant ''wast.'' ''Wyclif'', Gen. xvii. 14.
<poem>His ''waste'' wordes retournd to him in vaine.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. i. 42.}}}}
'''6.''' Exuberant; over-abundant; hence, superfluous; useless.
{{smaller block|<poem>Strangled with her ''waste'' fertility.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 729.}}}}
'''7†.''' Wasteful; prodigal; profuse.
{{smaller block|<poem>My ''waast'' expensis y wole with-drawe;
Now, certis, ''waast'' weel callid thei be,
For thei were spent my boost to blowe,
My name to bere bothe on londe & see.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 179.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To lay waste.''' See ''lay''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Waste-steam pipe''', in a steam-engine, a pipe for conveying away the steam that escapes through the safety-valve.}}

'''waste<sup>1</sup>''' (wāst), ''n.''   [< ME. ''waste'', < OF. ''wast'', a waste, ''guast'', ''gast'', ''vast'', waste, devastation; cf. MHG. ''waste'', a desert; forms confused with early ME. ''weste'', < AS. ''wēsten'' = OS. ''wōstun'' = OHG. ''wuostī'', MHG. ''wueste'', G. ''wüste'', a waste, desert: see ''waste''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'']   '''1.''' A wild, uninhabited, or desolate place or region; a desert; a wilderness.
{{smaller block|The world’s great ''waste'', the ocean.
{{right|''Waller'', To my Lord Protector.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>No other object breaks
The ''waste'' but one dwarf tree.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Julian and Maddalo.}}}}
{{smaller block|A dreary ''waste'', exhibiting scarcely a vestige of civilization. ''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., i. [The Barbary States were] bounded . . . on the south by the vast, indefinite, sandy, flinty ''wastes'' of Sahara.
{{right|''Sumner'', Orations, I. 205.}}}}
{{smaller block|Fancy flutters over these vague ''wastes'' like a butterfly blown out to sea, and finds no foothold.
{{right|''Lowell'', Harvard Anniversary.}}}}
'''2.''' Untilled or uncultivated ground; a tract of land not in a state of cultivation, and producing little or no herbage or wood.
{{smaller block|One small gate that open’d on the ''waste''.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''coal-mining'', gob; also, the fine coal made in mining and preparing coal for the market; culm; coal-dirt; dirt: in the Pennsylvania anthracite region, used to signify both the mine-waste (or coal left in the mine in pillars, etc.) and the breaker waste.—'''4.''' Gradual loss, diminution, or decay, as in bulk, substance, strength, or value, from continued use, wear, disease, etc.: as, ''waste'' of tissue; ''waste'' of energy.
{{smaller block|Beauty’s ''waste'' hath in the world an end.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, ix.}}}}
{{smaller block|Were Life uniform in its rate, . . . repair and ''waste'' of all organs, including nervous organs, would have to keep an approximately even pace, one with the other.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Psychol., § 37.}}}}
'''5.''' Consumption; decline; a pining away.
{{smaller block|There ’s many a one as works in a carding-room who falls into a ''waste'', coughing and spitting blood, because they’re just poisoned by the fluff.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', North and South, xiii.}}}}
'''6.''' Broken, spoiled, useless, or superfluous material; stuff that is left over, or that is unfitted or cannot readily be utilized for the purpose for which it was intended; overplus, useless, or rejected material; refuse, as the overflow water from a dam or reservoir, broken or spoiled castings in a foundry, paper scraps in a printing-office or bindery, or shreds of yarn in a cotton- or woolen-mill.
{{smaller block|What is called in typographical language the ''waste'' of works printed at the Academy is seldom or never preserved, as it ought to be.
{{right|''Rev. W. Tooke'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 430).}}}}
{{smaller block|“I don’t know how it is, sir,” said one ''waste'' collector, . . . “I can’t make it out, but paper gets scarcer or else I’m out of luck. Just at this time my family and me really couldn’t live on my ''waste'' if we had to depend entirely upon it.”
{{right|''Mayhew,'' London Labour and London Poor, II. 11.}}}}
'''7.''' Rubbish; trash; nonsense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why fader, in faith, are yo so fer troublet
At his wordys of ''waste,'' & his wit febill?</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2546.}}}}
'''8.''' A weir or sluice for carrying off the overflow from a dam, reservoir, or canal.—'''9.''' A waste-pipe, or any contrivance for allowing waste matter or surplus water, steam, etc., to escape.
{{smaller block|If more than one basin is fixed upon the same ''waste,'' the size should be proportionately increased.
{{right|''S. S. Hellyer,'' The Plumber, p. 47.}}}}
'''10.''' Unnecessary or useless expenditure: as, ''waste'' of time, labor, or money.
{{smaller block|So to order and dispende the same that no ''waste'' or vnprofitable excesse be made.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages,'' I. 227.}}}}
{{smaller block|Prefaces, and passages, and excusations, and other speeches of reference to the person, are great ''wastes'' of time.
{{right|''Bacon'', Dispatch (ed. 1887).}}}}

'''11.''' A superfluity.
{{smaller block|We’ll girt them with an ample ''waste'' of love.
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, I., i. 1.}}}}

'''12.''' In ''law'', anything suffered by a tenant in the nature of permanent injury to the inheritance, not occasioned by the act of God or a public enemy; the result of any act or omission by the tenant of a particular estate by which the estate of the remainder-man or reversioner is rendered less valuable.—'''Cotton waste.''' {{smaller|See ''cotton-waste''.}}—'''Equitable waste,''' {{smaller|injuries to the inheritance which fall short of waste as defined by the common law, but which a court of equity will treat as equivalent to waste.}}—'''Impeachment of waste.''' {{smaller|See ''impeachment''.}}—'''In waste†,''' {{smaller|in vain.}}
{{smaller block|Ich haue wrouȝt al ''in wast'' ac i nel na more.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 718.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thir wise wordis ware noght wroght ''in waste'',
To waffe and wende away als wynde.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 95.}}}}
'''Permissive waste,''' {{smaller|waste by omission to prevent it.}}—'''Tanners’ waste.''' {{smaller|See ''tanner''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''To run to waste,''' {{smaller|to become exhausted, useless, or spoiled, as from want of proper judgment, management, care, or skill; become lost for any useful purpose.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Alas! our young affections ''run to waste'',
Or water but the desert.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 120.}}}}
'''Voluntary waste.''' {{smaller|See ''voluntary''.}}—'''Waste-picking machine,''' {{smaller|a machine for shredding waste fabric into shoddy; a rag-picker.}}—'''Waster waste.''' {{smaller|See the quotation under ''waster''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 4 (''b'').}}='''Syn. 6.''' ''Refuse'', ''Damage'', etc. {{smaller|See ''loss''.}}

'''waste'''<sup>1</sup> (wāst), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wasted'', ppr. ''wasting''.   [< ME. ''wasten'', ''waasten'', < OF. ''waster'', ''guaster'', ''gaster'', F. ''gâter'', waste (= Pr. ''gastar'', ''guastar'' = Sp. Pg. ''gastar'' = It. ''guastare'', < MHG. ''wasten'', lay waste), < L. ''vastare'', waste, devastate, < ''vastus'', waste, desert: see ''waste''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', and cf. ''vastate'', ''devastate''. Cf. G. ''wüsten'', lay waste.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To lay waste; devastate; destroy; ruin.
{{smaller block|<poem>For-thi wiȝtli with werre i ''wasted'' alle hire londes,
& brouȝt hire at swiche bale that sche mercy craued.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4587.}}}}
{{smaller block|And at the Fote of this Hille was somtyme a gode Cytee of Cristene Men, that Men cleped Cayphas, For Cayphas first founded it; but it is now alle ''wasted''.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|Bathy sent Cadan to pursue the King into Sclauonia, still fleeing before him, who ''wasted'' Bosna, Seruia, and Bulgaria.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 405.}}}}
{{smaller block|He more ''wasted'' the Britains then any Saxon King before him.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., iv.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''law'', to damage, injure, or impair, as an estate, voluntarily, or by allowing the buildings, fences, etc., to fall into decay.—'''3.''' To diminish or reduce in bulk, substance, strength, value, or the like, as by continued use, wear, loss, decay, or disease; consume or wear away; use up; spend.
{{smaller block|Would he were ''wasted'', marrow, bones, and all!
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 125.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The span of time
Doth ''waste'' us to our graves.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|My heart is ''wasted'' with my woe.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Oriana.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
